<span id="what-is-the-meaning-of-the-estimation-error"></span>

### What is the meaning of the intra-document estimation error? {#what-is-the-meaning-of-the-meta-estimation-error .revision-section}

We start with an infinite exchangeable sequence of documents and hold its full joint law fixed while considering different choices of document parameters. Following Jeon et al., $D_m$ denotes document $m$, $\theta_m$ its document parameter, and $H_{M,T}=(D_1,\ldots,D_M)$ the complete corpus of $M$ documents of length $T$.

By de Finetti's theorem, there is a shared random variable $\rho$ that makes the documents conditionally iid, i.e. $D_1,D_2, \dots | \rho \text{i.i.d.}$. We write $f_\rho(d):=P(D_1=d\mid\rho)$ for the document distribution it determines. We can view $\rho$ as the Bayesian prior over a complete document. Consequently, a whole dataset would be one partially observed sample of the Bayesian prior.   

The following lemma shows that the resulting decomposition into estimation error and irreducible error depends only on the full joint law of the infinite document sequence, not on the choice of latent variable making the documents conditionally iid. 

#### Lemma B.1: the canonical de Finetti split

Fix the law of an infinite exchangeable sequence of complete documents $D_1,D_2,\ldots$ on the finite space $\Sigma^T$. Let $\rho$ be any random variable such that

$$
D_1,D_2,\ldots\mid\rho\quad\text{iid}.
$$

Then the split

$$
\underbrace{\frac{H(H_{M,T})}{MT}}_{L_{\mathrm{opt}}}
=\underbrace{\frac{I(H_{M,T};\rho)}{MT}}_{\substack{E_{\mathrm{can}}\\\text{canonical estimation error}}}
+\underbrace{\frac{H(D_m\mid\rho)}{T}}_{\substack{R_{\mathrm{can}}\\\text{canonical irreducible error}}}
$$

is determined by that document process. Both $E_{\mathrm{can}}$ and $R_{\mathrm{can}}$ stay fixed when we change its latent representation. 

**Proof.** Let $\tau$ be another random variable such that $D_1,D_2,\ldots\mid\tau$ are iid, and define

$$
f_\rho(d):=P(D_1=d\mid\rho),
\qquad
f_\tau(d):=P(D_1=d\mid\tau).
$$

By uniqueness in [Theorem 1 of Barber, Candès, Ramdas, and Tibshirani](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~ryantibs/papers/defin.pdf#page=5), $f_\rho$ and $f_\tau$ have the same law. Thus, writing $h(f)$ for the entropy of a document distribution $f$,

$$
H(H_{M,T}\mid\rho)
=M\mathbb E[h(f_\rho)]
=M\mathbb E[h(f_\tau)]
=H(H_{M,T}\mid\tau).
$$

The corpus law is fixed, so $H(H_{M,T})$ is unchanged. Subtracting the equal conditional entropies gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
I(H_{M,T};\rho)
&=H(H_{M,T})-H(H_{M,T}\mid\rho)\\
&=H(H_{M,T})-H(H_{M,T}\mid\tau)\\
&=I(H_{M,T};\tau).
\end{aligned}
$$

These equalities fix both terms of the split. $\square$

#### How does Jeon et al.'s estimation-error decomposition relate to Lemma B.1? 


Keep the joint law of $\psi$ and the documents fixed, with the documents iid given $\psi$, and write $f_\psi(d):=P(D_m=d\mid\psi)$. Applying Lemma B.1 with $\tau=\psi$ gives

$$
\frac{I(H_{M,T};\psi)}{MT}=E_{\mathrm{can}}.
$$

Thus, Jeon et al.'s meta estimation error is the canonical estimation error. They also assume that the document parameters $\theta_m$ are iid given $\psi$, and that $D_m\perp\psi\mid\theta_m$.

Jeon et al. call the uncertainty that remains when $\psi$ and the document parameters are known the **irreducible error**. Its per-token value is

$$
\frac{H(H_{M,T}\mid\psi,\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_M)}{MT}
=\frac{H(D_m\mid\theta_m)}{T}.
$$

Jeon et al. define their optimal estimation error $\mathcal L_{M,T}$ as the optimal prediction loss minus this irreducible error. Theorem Jeon.4.2 gives

$$
\underbrace{\frac{H(H_{M,T})}{MT}}_{\substack{\text{optimal}\\\text{prediction loss}}}
=\underbrace{
\underbrace{\frac{I(H_{M,T};\psi)}{MT}}_{\substack{\text{meta estimation error}\\=E_{\mathrm{can}}}}
+\underbrace{\frac{I(D_m;\theta_m\mid\psi)}{T}}_{\substack{\text{intra-document}\\\text{estimation error}}}
}_{\mathcal L_{M,T}:\ \text{estimation error}}
+\underbrace{\frac{H(D_m\mid\theta_m)}{T}}_{\text{irreducible error}}.
$$

The document parameters split the canonical irreducible error as follows:

$$
R_{\mathrm{can}}=\frac{H(D_m\mid\psi)}{T}
=\underbrace{\frac{I(D_m;\theta_m\mid\psi)}{T}}_{\text{intra-document estimation error}}
+\underbrace{\frac{H(D_m\mid\theta_m)}{T}}_{\text{irreducible error}}.
$$

So Jeon et al.'s estimation error is the meta estimation error plus the intra-document estimation error. The meta term stays fixed with the document process, while the split of $R_{\mathrm{can}}$ between intra-document estimation error and irreducible error can depend on the choice of $\theta_m$.

#### Two extreme examples: $\theta_m=\psi$ and $\theta_m=D_m$

There are not enough restrictions on $\theta_m$ in the general framework to obtain an intra-document estimation error that is determined by the distribution of the document sequence. E.g. we may choose $\theta_m=\psi$, or at the other extreme $\theta_m=D_m$.

**Choice 1: $\theta_m=\psi$.** Give every document parameter exactly the shared information. Given $\psi$, choose the sole available parameter $\theta_m=\psi$, then generate the complete document from $f_\psi$. This is precisely the original conditional document distribution, with any former document-specific latent variable integrated out. Now

$$
\underbrace{I(D_m;\theta_m\mid\psi)}_{\text{intra-document information}}
=I(D_m;\psi\mid\psi)=0,
\qquad H(D_m\mid\theta_m)=H(D_m\mid\psi).
$$

**Choice 2: $\theta_m=D_m$.** Given $\psi$, draw a document-valued parameter $\theta_m\sim f_\psi$, then output $D_m=\theta_m$. The document has exactly the same law as before, but knowing its parameter now determines it completely:

$$
\underbrace{I(D_m;\theta_m\mid\psi)}_{\text{intra-document information}}
=I(D_m;D_m\mid\psi)=H(D_m\mid\psi),
\qquad H(D_m\mid\theta_m)=0.
$$

The resulting quantities are:

| Document parameter | Meta $=E_{\mathrm{can}}$ | Intra-document | Jeon et al.'s irreducible error | Jeon et al.'s total $\mathcal L_{M,T}$ |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| $\theta_m=\psi$ | unchanged | $0$ | $R_{\mathrm{can}}$ | $E_{\mathrm{can}}$ |
| $\theta_m=D_m$ | unchanged | $R_{\mathrm{can}}$ | $0$ | $E_{\mathrm{can}}+R_{\mathrm{can}}=L_{\mathrm{opt}}$ |

A zero irreducible error in Jeon et al. means $\theta_m$ determines the whole document; the canonical irreducible error $R_{\mathrm{can}}$ has not vanished. These are alternative latent representations. An invertible reparameterization alone cannot change mutual information.

#### Do Jeon et al.'s assumptions allow this? [@jeon2024information]

Yes, under the general requirements of Section 4.1. Here is the check from my attachment, with its autoregressive step repaired:

| Requirement | $\theta_m=\psi$ | $\theta_m=D_m$ |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Exchangeable documents, iid given $\psi$ | The joint law of $(\psi,D_1,D_2,\ldots)$ stays fixed. | The same conditional law $f_\psi$ is sampled independently for each document. |
| $\theta_1,\theta_2,\ldots\mid\psi$ iid | $\psi,\psi,\ldots\mid\psi$ are iid: a point mass is allowed. | The parameters are independent draws from $f_\psi$. |
| $D_m\perp\psi\mid\theta_m$ | $D_m\perp\psi\mid\psi$. | $D_m\perp\psi\mid D_m$. |
| Autoregressive generation; discrete tokens and length $T$ | Generate from $f_\psi$ using its token conditionals. | Emit the stored document token by token. |
| Independence across documents given $\psi$ | Use independent document draws. | Use independent parameter draws. |

<summary>Technical detail: autoregressive generation and the attachment's gap</summary>

For finite $\Sigma$, every document law $r$ on $\Sigma^T$ has an autoregressive generator. If $r[h]$ denotes the probability of prefix $h$, use

$$
A_r(h)(x)=\begin{cases}
r[hx]/r[h],&r[h]>0,\\
1/|\Sigma|,&r[h]=0.
\end{cases}
$$

This reproduces $r$; zero-probability prefixes are never reached. Apply it to $r=f_\psi$ in the first choice and $r=\delta_{\theta_m}$ in the second. On standard Borel parameter spaces these finite sums and piecewise ratios are measurable. No encoding of infinite sequences or differential entropy is needed.

The attachment's item (ii) demanded strict dependence at every token position. De Finetti does not establish that: it concerns independence **across documents**, not dependence inside a document. Jeon et al.'s Section 3 says the next token “may depend” on the parameter and history; its general framework states no strict information inequality excluding these endpoints. The check above uses conditional kernels instead of that extra premise. The description of parameters as document-specific would need an additional formal restriction to exclude $\theta_m=\psi$.

#### What follows for the interpretation?

In Section 4.6, Jeon et al. [@jeon2024information] argue that the in-context estimation error can be small even for short contexts. Under their transformer-mixture model, the context only needs to distinguish which of the $N$ models generated the document, giving a bound of $\log(N)/\tau$.

The meta-estimation term is canonical, as established above. However, the intra-document term depends on the choice of $\theta_m$, not just on the document distribution. Its smallness therefore cannot, by itself, establish a statement about the document distribution alone: that in-context learning is intrinsically easy. Changing $\theta_m$ also changes the irreducible error against which performance is measured. 

One may fix the intra document estimation error, applying a possible restriction to $\theta_m$, by requiring it contain no oracle information. 
To make this precise, consider predicting a new document $D_{M+1}$ after observing the training corpus $H_{M,T}$. Define the oracle advantage as the reduction in optimal expected log loss obtained by additionally revealing its parameter:

$$
O_M:=\frac1T\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}
I\!\left(X_{t+1}^{(M+1)};\theta_{M+1}
\mid H_{M,T},X_{1:t}^{(M+1)}\right)
=\frac{I(D_{M+1};\theta_{M+1}\mid H_{M,T})}{T}.
$$

This compares predictions based on the training corpus and observed context with predictions that also have privileged access to the document parameter. For a finite corpus, that access may also compensate for incomplete knowledge of the shared document distribution. To exclude only an advantage that persists after arbitrarily much training data, we impose $\lim_{M\to\infty}O_M=0$.

$$
O_M
=\frac{I(D_{M+1};\psi\mid H_{M,T})}{T}
+\frac{I(D_{M+1};\theta_{M+1}\mid\psi)}{T}.
$$

For our finite document space, the first term tends to zero as the training corpus determines $f_\psi$. The second is the same for every document. Consequently,

$$
\lim_{M\to\infty}O_M
=\underbrace{\frac{I(D_m;\theta_m\mid\psi)}{T}}_{\text{intra-document estimation error}}.
$$

Our no-oracle restriction therefore implies that the intra-document estimation error is zero. 
This does not mean that context is useless. Knowing $f_\psi$ already determines how an observed prefix changes predictions for its continuation, including any inference about document-specific parameters from that prefix. 

The [diagram](#bowls) illustrates how the choice of $\theta_m$ divides the fixed residual $R_{\mathrm{can}}$ into intra-document estimation error and irreducible error. Under the restriction above, the entire residual is irreducible error.
